stem: An ACL contains, in order: (1) permit tcp 10.0.0.0/8 to 10.5.5.5 port 443, (2) deny tcp 10.1.2.3 to 10.5.5.5 port 443. Host 10.1.2.3 can still reach the server. Why?

options.text: Rule 1 matches the traffic first, so rule 2 is never evaluated
options.why: ACLs are evaluated top to bottom and stop at the first match. The specific deny must be placed above the broader permit.

options.text: Deny rules require an explicit log keyword before they take effect
options.why: Logging is unrelated to enforcement. The rule never runs, which is an ordering problem.

options.text: The implicit deny at the end overrides explicit deny rules
options.why: The implicit deny only applies to traffic that matched nothing. It does not override anything.

options.text: Host rules cannot override subnet rules on a stateful firewall
options.why: They can, provided they are placed above the subnet rule. Position is what decides, not specificity.

stem: You must permit an entire subnet to reach a file server, except one quarantined host. How should the rules be ordered?

options.text: Deny the quarantined host first, then permit the subnet
options.why: Specific before general. The exception must be evaluated before the broad rule that would otherwise match it.

options.text: Permit the subnet first, then deny the quarantined host
options.why: The permit matches the quarantined host too, so the deny below it can never fire.

options.text: Order does not matter because deny always takes precedence over permit
options.why: There is no precedence by action. There is only position, and the first match wins.

options.text: Permit the subnet and rely on the implicit deny to exclude the host
options.why: The implicit deny catches only unmatched traffic. The quarantined host matches the permit.

stem: A requirements document ends with 'all other traffic must be denied'. The firewall is a standard stateful device. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Nothing is strictly required, though an explicit deny any at the bottom is worth adding so drops are logged
options.why: Every ACL already ends in an implicit deny. The explicit rule adds visibility, which is the real reason to write it.

options.text: Add a permit any any rule at the bottom to make the behaviour explicit
options.why: This permits everything the requirements forbid and renders the rest of the rule set meaningless.

options.text: Nothing, because denied traffic is logged automatically by the implicit deny
options.why: The implicit deny generally does not log. That is precisely why administrators add an explicit deny.

options.text: Set the firewall's default policy to permit and add individual deny rules
options.why: This inverts the security model, requiring you to enumerate every bad thing rather than permitting only what is needed.

stem: Internet users must reach a public web server at 203.0.113.10 over HTTPS. Which rule is correct?

options.text: permit tcp any any -> 203.0.113.10 port 443
options.why: The destination is the server and the destination port is the service. The client's source port is ephemeral, so it is any.

options.text: permit tcp any port 443 -> 203.0.113.10 any
options.why: This puts the service port on the source side. It matches only traffic coming from something whose source port is 443, which is the server's replies, not client requests.

options.text: permit tcp 203.0.113.10 port 443 -> any any
options.why: This is written in the reverse direction. Rules are written in the direction the connection is initiated.

options.text: permit tcp any any -> 203.0.113.10 any
options.why: This permits every TCP port on the server, not just HTTPS. It works, and it exposes SSH, RDP and everything else.

stem: On a stateful firewall you permit internal clients outbound to TCP 443. A colleague asks whether a second rule is needed to permit the replies back in. What is the correct answer?

options.text: No. The firewall tracks the connection in its state table and permits the return traffic automatically
options.why: That is the defining behaviour of a stateful firewall: one rule per connection, written in the direction it is initiated.

options.text: Yes, a matching inbound rule from any port 443 to the internal subnet is required
options.why: On a stateful device this is an unnecessary inbound opening, and it permits unsolicited inbound traffic from anything sourcing port 443.

options.text: Yes, but only if the connection uses TLS
options.why: State tracking is independent of the application protocol carried inside the connection.

options.text: No, because the implicit deny does not apply to return traffic
options.why: The right answer, wrong reason. Return traffic is permitted by the state table, not by an exception to the implicit deny.

stem: A public web server in the screened subnet needs to query an internal database. Which rule best satisfies the requirement without weakening the zone design?

options.text: permit tcp WEB-SRV any -> DB-SRV port 1433
options.why: One host, one destination, one port. The screened subnet is permitted exactly the one flow the application needs and nothing else.

options.text: permit tcp DMZ-NET any -> INTERNAL-NET any
options.why: This lets any compromised host in the screened subnet reach anything inside, which is the exact pivot the zone exists to prevent.

options.text: permit tcp WEB-SRV any -> INTERNAL-NET port 1433
options.why: Closer, but it permits the web server to reach every internal host on 1433, not just the one database it needs.

options.text: permit ip any any between the screened subnet and the internal network
options.why: This removes the boundary entirely and makes the screened subnet an extension of the internal network.

stem: Which traffic direction should normally be denied in a screened subnet design?

options.text: Screened subnet hosts initiating connections into the internal network
options.why: Public facing hosts are the most likely to be compromised, so they must not be able to open connections toward the more trusted zone except for narrowly named flows.

options.text: Internal hosts initiating connections into the screened subnet
options.why: Trust flows from more trusted to less trusted. Internal administrators and users routinely need to reach these servers.

options.text: The internet initiating connections to published services in the screened subnet
options.why: That is the entire purpose of the zone. Blocking it would take the public services offline.

options.text: Screened subnet hosts initiating connections to the internet
options.why: This is often restricted, but it is not the defining rule of the design. The critical denial is toward the internal network.

stem: A requirement states that the jump host at 10.20.5.15 is the only system permitted to administer servers over SSH. An engineer writes: permit tcp 10.20.0.0/16 any -> SERVERS port 22. An audit fails the rule. Why?

options.text: It permits the whole internal network, not the single named host, violating least privilege
options.why: The required traffic works, which is why this error survives testing. Any workstation on the internal network can now administer the servers.

options.text: The destination port should be the source port for SSH
options.why: The destination port is correct at 22. The defect is the breadth of the source.

options.text: SSH rules must specify UDP as well as TCP
options.why: SSH is TCP only. Adding UDP would broaden the rule further without purpose.

options.text: An explicit deny for all other hosts is missing below it
options.why: No such rule is needed. Anything not permitted is already denied. The problem is that too much has been permitted.

stem: A public web application is being targeted by SQL injection and cross site scripting attempts against its search parameter. Which control is designed for this?

options.text: A web application firewall
options.why: A WAF inspects HTTP requests, parameters and payloads, which is the layer these attacks operate at.

options.text: A next-generation firewall with application awareness
options.why: An NGFW is the broader and more capable perimeter device, and its IPS may catch some attempts. For attacks against one application's parameters, the specialised device is correct.

options.text: A unified threat management appliance
options.why: UTM bundles many functions for a small site. It is a breadth answer to a depth problem.

options.text: A stateful firewall permitting only 443 to the server
options.why: The attack arrives inside permitted HTTPS traffic. A port based rule cannot see it.

stem: Management requires that known exploit traffic be blocked in real time before reaching internal servers. Which deployment meets the requirement?

options.text: An IPS deployed inline in the traffic path
options.why: Only a device that the traffic actually passes through can drop it. Inline placement is what makes prevention possible.

options.text: An IDS connected to a SPAN port on the core switch
options.why: A SPAN port delivers a copy of the traffic after the fact. The device can alert but the original packets have already been delivered.

options.text: An IDS inline with alerting configured to page the on-call engineer
options.why: An IDS detects. Placing it inline does not give it the ability to drop traffic, and it adds a failure point.

options.text: A passive network tap feeding a SIEM with automated ticket creation
options.why: Passive means out of band. Tickets are created after the traffic has already arrived.

stem: A small business owner states that their office is safe from inbound attacks because the router performs NAT. How should this be assessed?

options.text: NAT is not a security control; a firewall policy is still required
options.why: NAT translates addresses. Unsolicited inbound connections have nowhere to land by default, but nothing is being evaluated against a policy, and any forwarded port bypasses the effect entirely.

options.text: Correct, NAT provides equivalent protection to a stateful firewall
options.why: NAT makes no policy decisions, logs nothing, and does not restrict outbound traffic at all.

options.text: Correct for inbound traffic, though outbound filtering should be added
options.why: This concedes the premise. The inbound protection is a side effect of address translation, not an enforced policy.

options.text: NAT is a compensating control that satisfies the firewall requirement
options.why: A compensating control must actually achieve the objective by another means. NAT does not evaluate traffic against a policy.

stem: After a change, an administrator notices that the last four rules in a 30 rule ACL appear never to increment their hit counters. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A broader rule higher in the list already matches that traffic, so those rules are unreachable
options.why: This is rule shadowing. The rules are present and correct in isolation, and they can never execute.

options.text: Hit counters do not increment on deny rules
options.why: Counters increment on any rule that matches, regardless of action.

options.text: The rules are below the implicit deny and are therefore skipped
options.why: The implicit deny is always last by definition. No configured rule can be below it.

options.text: The firewall only evaluates the first 16 rules of any ACL
options.why: There is no such limit. The behaviour is explained by ordering, not by a cap.

stem: Internal workstations must be permitted to resolve names against an external DNS resolver at 9.9.9.9. Which rule is correct?

options.text: permit udp INTERNAL-NET any -> 9.9.9.9 port 53
options.why: DNS queries are UDP 53 to the resolver. The client's source port is ephemeral.

options.text: permit udp INTERNAL-NET port 53 -> 9.9.9.9 any
options.why: This places the service port on the source side. Clients do not source from port 53.

options.text: permit udp any any -> any port 53
options.why: This permits every host to query every DNS server on the internet, which defeats the point of naming a specific approved resolver.

options.text: permit tcp INTERNAL-NET any -> 9.9.9.9 port 53
options.why: TCP 53 is used for zone transfers and large responses, not for ordinary client queries. Permitting only TCP would break normal resolution.

stem: Which capability distinguishes a next-generation firewall from a traditional stateful firewall?

options.text: It identifies the application and the user behind the traffic, not merely the port and protocol
options.why: Application and identity awareness, usually with integrated intrusion prevention, is what defines an NGFW.

options.text: It tracks connection state so return traffic is permitted automatically
options.why: That is the definition of a stateful firewall, which an NGFW also does. It is not what makes it next generation.

options.text: It performs address translation for internal hosts
options.why: NAT is available on almost any router or firewall and is not a security differentiator.

options.text: It provides deep inspection of one web application's parameters
options.why: That depth on a single application is a WAF's specialisation.

stem: During a firewall review, which finding indicates a least privilege problem rather than a functional problem?

options.text: A rule permits the required flow and also permits a wide range of unrelated traffic
options.why: Everything works, so testing passes. The rule grants more than the requirement asked for, which is precisely a least privilege failure.

options.text: A required application is unreachable because no rule permits it
options.why: That is a functional gap. Nothing has been over-permitted.

options.text: A deny rule appears below a permit rule that already matches the same traffic
options.why: That is an ordering defect. It may cause over-permission, but the finding is that the rule is unreachable.

options.text: The ACL has no explicit deny statement at the end
options.why: That is a logging gap. The traffic is still denied implicitly.

stem: An inline IPS protects a payment processing segment. The security team must decide its behaviour if the appliance fails. Which consideration is most relevant?

options.text: Fail-closed protects the segment but causes an outage; fail-open preserves availability but leaves traffic uninspected
options.why: This is the core trade-off of inline placement, and the right answer depends on whether confidentiality or availability dominates for that segment.

options.text: The question does not arise, because an IPS is deployed out of band
options.why: An IPS must be inline to drop traffic. Out of band placement describes an IDS.

options.text: Failure has no effect because the stateful firewall continues to filter
options.why: The firewall filters by policy. It does not perform the signature and behaviour inspection the IPS was deployed for.

options.text: Fail-open should always be selected to maintain availability
options.why: For a payment segment, uninspected traffic may be the less acceptable risk. There is no universal default.

stem: An ACL begins with: permit ip any any, followed by twelve carefully scoped rules and an explicit deny. What is the effect?

options.text: All traffic is permitted, and the remaining rules never execute
options.why: The first rule matches everything, so evaluation stops there for every packet. The rest of the list is decoration.

options.text: Traffic is permitted only if it also matches one of the twelve scoped rules
options.why: Evaluation stops at the first match. Rules are not combined.

options.text: The explicit deny at the end overrides the permit at the top
options.why: There is no precedence by position at the end. Only the first match matters.

options.text: The firewall rejects the configuration as contradictory
options.why: It is a valid configuration. It is simply a completely permissive one.

stem: A 20 person office with no IT staff needs perimeter filtering, antivirus, web filtering, VPN termination and intrusion prevention, managed through one interface and one licence. Which is the best fit?

options.text: A unified threat management appliance
options.why: UTM exists exactly for this case: many security functions consolidated into a single box and a single management surface for a small site.

options.text: A web application firewall
options.why: A WAF protects a web application the organisation publishes. It does none of the perimeter functions listed.

options.text: Separate best of breed appliances for each function
options.why: Technically stronger and unmanageable for an office with no IT staff, which is the constraint in the stem.

options.text: A stateless packet filtering router
options.why: It provides none of the listed functions and would require reverse rules for every flow.
